title.zh: 头痛怎么办？试试这4个穴位

description.zh: 介绍4个有效缓解头痛的穴位及其按摩方法，帮助您快速缓解头痛不适
description.en: Four effective acupoints for headache relief and massage techniques

zh.text: 头痛是临床极为常见的病症，也是我在门诊中几乎每天都会遇到的诉求。《黄帝内经》将头痛归为"首风""脑风"范畴，认为其病机不外乎外感和内伤两端——外感多为风、寒、湿等邪气侵袭经络，内伤则与肝阳上亢、气血亏虚、痰浊阻络密切相关。穴位按摩作为中医外治法的一种，对于缓解各类头痛有着确切的疗效，且操作简便，患者可自行实施。
太阳穴是经外奇穴，位于眉梢与外眼角之间向后约1寸的凹陷处。此穴是治疗头痛的要穴，尤其擅长疏风止痛、清头明目。我在临床上常对偏头痛、紧张性头痛的患者首推此穴，特别是因长时间用眼、视疲劳引发的前额及颞侧疼痛，按压太阳穴往往能快速缓解。按摩时用拇指或食指指腹按压，力度适中，以局部有酸胀感为佳，顺时针揉按1至2分钟即可。
风池穴属足少阳胆经，位于后颈部枕骨下方、两侧肌肉凹陷处。"风池"之名寓意其为风邪易袭之所，因此该穴擅长疏风解表、清头止痛。《针灸甲乙经》记载风池可治"头痛、目眩"。对于风寒感冒初起伴有头痛、颈项强痛的患者，按揉风池穴效果显著，尤其适合长期伏案工作导致的颈源性头痛。按摩时用双手拇指按压，自下而上推揉，每次2至3分钟，往往能感到一股暖流从后脑传至头顶。
百会穴位于督脉之上，在头顶正中，两耳尖连线的中点处。"百会"意为百脉之会，是诸阳之会，有升阳举陷、醒脑开窍之功。在临床中，我常用百会穴治疗头晕头痛兼有失眠健忘的患者。该穴对于气血亏虚所致的头痛尤为适宜，此类患者常伴有面色苍白、头晕目眩、劳累后加重等表现。按摩时用中指或拇指轻轻揉按，每次1至2分钟，力度不宜过重。

合谷穴是大肠经的原穴，位于手背第一、二掌骨之间，约第二掌骨中点处。《针灸甲乙经》称合谷"主头痛、目痛、齿痛"，是四总穴之一——"面口合谷收"。此穴功效全面，能疏风解表、镇痛安神，适用于多种类型的头痛，尤其以前头痛和眉棱骨痛最为有效。我在临床中发现，对于因感冒、鼻窦炎引起的前额疼痛，合谷配合迎香穴使用效果更佳。按摩时用拇指按压对侧手背的合谷穴，力度以有酸胀感为宜，每次3至5分钟。需要提醒的是，孕妇禁用此穴。
《伤寒论》中系统论述了六经头痛的辨治思路，对临床选穴有重要指导意义。根据头痛部位的不同，选穴侧重点也有所区别：前额及眉棱骨痛属阳明经头痛，以合谷穴为主配合足三里；偏头痛属少阳经头痛，以太阳穴为主配合风池穴；后头痛连及项部属太阳经头痛，以风池穴为主；巅顶痛属厥阴经头痛，以百会穴为主。全头痛或部位不固定者，可综合使用上述四个穴位。这样的配穴思路既体现了经络辨证的精准性，也兼顾了治疗的便捷性。

穴位按摩虽简便易行，但也要注意方法得当。按摩时应保持全身放松，呼吸自然，切忌急躁。力度宜由轻渐重，以局部出现酸、麻、胀感为宜，切勿用力过猛以免造成损伤。每个穴位按摩1至3分钟即可，单次总时长控制在20分钟内。可配合热敷，先热敷再按摩，效果更佳——热敷能促进局部气血流通，使穴位更加敏感。需要强调的是，穴位按摩贵在持之以恒，每日坚持才能巩固疗效。若头痛频繁发作、程度剧烈或伴有恶心呕吐、肢体麻木等症状，务必及时就医做进一步检查，以排除颅内病变等严重疾患。
温馨提示：穴位按摩适用于日常保健和轻度头痛缓解。如头痛频繁发作、程度剧烈或伴有意识改变、肢体活动障碍等，应立即就医，查明头痛的根本原因。

en.text: Headache is one of the most common clinical complaints, and one I encounter nearly every day in my practice. The Huangdi Neijing categorizes headache under 'head wind' and 'brain wind,' attributing its pathogenesis to two broad categories: external contraction and internal injury. External headaches arise from wind, cold, or dampness invading the meridians, while internal headaches are closely tied to liver yang rising, qi and blood deficiency, or phlegm-turbidity obstructing the collaterals. Acupoint massage, as a TCM external therapy, offers reliable relief for various types of headaches and is simple enough for patients to perform on their own.

Taiyang is an extraordinary point located in the depression about 1 cun behind the midpoint between the outer eyebrow tip and the outer eye corner. This is a key point for treating headaches, especially effective for dispersing wind, relieving pain, and clearing the head and eyes. In clinical practice, I recommend this point first for patients with migraines and tension headaches, particularly those caused by prolonged eye strain. Pressing Taiyang often brings rapid relief. Massage with the thumb or index finger pad at moderate pressure until local soreness is felt, rubbing clockwise for 1 to 2 minutes.

Fengchi belongs to the Gallbladder meridian and is located below the occipital bone at the back of the neck, in the depressions on both sides of the neck muscles. The name 'Fengchi' (Wind Pool) signifies that it is a place where wind pathogens readily accumulate, making it excellent for releasing wind, clearing the exterior, relieving head pain, and brightening the eyes. The Zhenjiu Jiayi Jing records Fengchi for treating 'headache and dizziness.' It is particularly effective for early-stage wind-cold common cold with headache and neck stiffness, as well as cervicogenic headaches from prolonged desk work. Press with both thumbs, pushing upward from below, for 2 to 3 minutes each time. Patients often report a warm sensation rising from the back of the head to the crown.

Baihui lies on the Governing Vessel at the crown of the head, precisely at the midpoint of the line connecting the tips of both ears. The name 'Baihui' means 'convergence of a hundred vessels,' and as the meeting point of all yang channels, it has the function of raising yang, lifting sunken qi, and awakening the mind. In clinical practice, I often use Baihui for patients with dizziness and headache accompanied by insomnia and poor memory. It is especially suitable for headache due to qi and blood deficiency, in which patients typically present with a pale complexion, dizziness, and worsening of symptoms after exertion. Massage gently with the middle finger or thumb for 1 to 2 minutes each time, using light pressure.

Hegu is the yuan-source point of the Large Intestine meridian, located on the dorsum of the hand between the first and second metacarpal bones, approximately at the midpoint of the second metacarpal. The Zhenjiu Jiayi Jing states that Hegu 'governs headache, eye pain, and tooth pain,' and it is one of the four master acupoints — captured in the classic saying 'facial and oral disorders are treated with Hegu.' This versatile point releases wind, clears the exterior, relieves pain, and calms the spirit. It is effective for many types of headache, particularly frontal headaches and supraorbital pain. In my clinical observation, combining Hegu with Yingxiang (LI20) yields especially good results for frontal pain caused by colds or sinusitis. Press Hegu on the opposite hand with the thumb until soreness is felt, 3 to 5 minutes each time. Caution: this point should be avoided during pregnancy.

The Shanghan Lun systematically discusses the differentiation and treatment of the six-meridian headaches, providing important guidance for clinical acupoint selection. Based on the location of the headache, the focus of point selection varies: frontal and supraorbital pain belongs to Yangming meridian headache and is treated primarily with Hegu, assisted by Zusanli; unilateral headache (migraine) belongs to Shaoyang meridian headache, treated primarily with Taiyang and assisted by Fengchi; posterior headache extending to the neck belongs to Taiyang meridian headache, treated primarily with Fengchi; vertex pain belongs to Jueyin meridian headache, treated primarily with Baihui. For whole-head pain or headache with unfixed location, all four points can be used in combination. This approach reflects both the precision of meridian differentiation and the convenience of practical treatment.

While acupoint massage is simple and accessible, proper technique matters. Keep your whole body relaxed and breathe naturally during massage, avoiding haste. Pressure should start light and gradually increase, aiming for local soreness, numbness, or distension — never apply excessive force that could cause injury. Massage each point for 1 to 3 minutes, keeping the total session within 20 minutes. Combining massage with a warm compress — apply the compress first, then massage — enhances results by promoting local qi and blood circulation and making the acupoints more responsive. Consistency is key: daily practice is needed to consolidate the therapeutic effect. If headaches become frequent, severe, or are accompanied by nausea, vomiting, or limb numbness, seek prompt medical examination to rule out serious intracranial conditions.

Note: Acupoint massage is suitable for daily health maintenance and mild headache relief. For frequent or severe headaches, or those accompanied by altered consciousness or motor impairment, seek immediate medical attention to determine the root cause.
